analysis.one_liner: Bans all oil, gas, and mineral leasing in the Arctic Ocean permanently.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred oil and gas drilling in the Arctic Ocean, never left the Senate Energy Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to permanently prohibit the Interior Department from issuing or extending any lease or authorization for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in Arctic areas of the Outer Continental Shelf [S2][S3]. No drilling company could ever get a federal permit to extract oil or gas from the Arctic Ocean off Alaska. The bill was introduced in November 2023, referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended in January 2025 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone exposed to climate change and oil spill risk from Arctic drilling gains: a permanent statutory ban would prevent new offshore extraction in a fragile, hard-to-clean-up ocean environment. Coastal and Indigenous communities in the Arctic region would face reduced spill and industrial-traffic risk [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities and the climate-exposed public

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes a permanent prohibition into law: the Interior Secretary 'shall not issue or extend a lease or any other authorization' for exploration, development, or production of oil, gas, or any other mineral in Arctic areas of the Outer Continental Shelf, and the ban overrides any other provision of law [S3].

Unlike a presidential withdrawal of offshore areas, which a future administration can reverse, a statutory ban would require Congress itself to repeal it, making the protection durable across administrations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose access to any future Arctic Ocean leases and the reserves they might contain. Drilling opponents also acknowledge that the United States forgoes potential domestic energy production, though the Arctic Outer Continental Shelf is not currently a major source of US output [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers seeking Arctic leases

drawbacks.text: The ban permanently locks away domestic energy resources; opponents of Arctic drilling restrictions argue the US should not unilaterally restrict its own oil and gas supply while global demand persists, and that restrictions push production to countries with weaker environmental rules [S2].

A permanent statutory ban removes the flexibility to revisit the decision if technology, economics, or energy-security conditions change, since the prohibition expressly overrides 'any other provision of this Act or any other law' [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is a permanent, hard-to-reverse environmental protection in a region where an oil spill would be extraordinarily difficult to clean up, and where new extraction would add to long-term climate risk. The cost is forgone potential domestic oil and gas supply, though the Arctic offshore is not currently a significant part of US production. The main design trade-off is permanence: the same override language that makes the protection durable also removes any flexibility to revisit it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the Stop Arctic Ocean Drilling Act of 2023 in the Senate on November 2, 2023, joined by seven original cosponsors [S1][S5].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, which is the last recorded action in its two-year life [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired on January 3, 2025 with the end of the 118th Congress [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers keep the possibility of future Arctic Ocean leases, and the ban's supporters keep nothing but the ability to reintroduce the bill in a future Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers; the ban died

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.role: Senator from Oregon and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban Arctic Outer Continental Shelf oil, gas, and mineral leasing.

for.name: Sen. Ed Markey
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor of the bill.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor of the bill.

for.name: 6 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 Senate Independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Sens. Wyden, Blumenthal, Welch, Sanders, Menendez alongside the original sponsors).

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee where the bill sat
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it received no committee action after referral and died at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never allowed the bill floor time; as the party holding procedural control of the chamber's calendar, no Arctic drilling ban reached the floor in the 118th Congress.

against.name: Oil and gas industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed statutory bans on Arctic offshore leasing, arguing the federal government should keep the Arctic Outer Continental Shelf open for energy development.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors were Democrats or allied Independents, with no Republican cosponsors, and the Democratic-controlled Senate committee never advanced the bill to the floor.

industries.industry: Oil and gas exploration and production companies
industries.note: The bill would permanently close the Arctic Outer Continental Shelf to new leases and drilling authorizations, eliminating any future revenue from those federal waters. The public benefit the bill offers — avoiding spill risk and new carbon extraction — is exactly the industry's forgone opportunity, so its interest runs against the bill's purpose.

industries.industry: Offshore drilling services and equipment suppliers
industries.note: A permanent leasing ban eliminates the prospect of future exploration and development contracts in Arctic waters, a small but high-value segment of the offshore services market.
